cards.front: How does a sedative differ from a hypnotic, and where does general anaesthesia fit?
cards.back: A sedative calms and reduces excitement, often with drowsiness but without true sleep, and has a flatter dose-response curve. A hypnotic induces and maintains sleep that resembles normal arousable sleep, with quicker onset, shorter action and a steeper dose-response curve. Sedation, hypnosis and general anaesthesia are increasing grades of CNS depression, and the drugs overlap; a hypnotic given at high dose can produce anaesthesia.

cards.front: Describe the normal sleep cycle: its stages and approximate length.
cards.back: Non-REM stages 1 to 4 are followed by REM sleep, and the cycle repeats every 80 to 100 minutes. Stage 2 is the largest share of sleep (about 40 to 50%). Stages 3 and 4 together form slow-wave sleep. REM sleep is about 20 to 30% of sleep, with irregular breathing, fluctuating heart rate, dreaming and full muscle relaxation.

cards.front: Classify: sleep stages
cards.text: Stage {{2}} forms the largest share of sleep (about {{40 to 50%}}), stages {{3 and 4}} together are called {{slow-wave sleep}}, and {{REM}} sleep takes about {{20 to 30%}} of the night.

cards.front: How do barbiturates act on the GABA-A receptor, and how does this differ from benzodiazepines?
cards.back: Barbiturates bind a site on the GABA-A chloride channel complex that is separate from the benzodiazepine site. They prolong the time the channel stays open, whereas benzodiazepines increase how often it opens. At high concentrations barbiturates can open the chloride channel directly, which benzodiazepines cannot do. This direct effect helps explain the higher depressant ceiling of barbiturates.

cards.front: What happens to sleep on repeated barbiturate use, and what follows withdrawal?
cards.back: Barbiturates shorten sleep onset and reduce night waking, but they suppress REM and deep (stage 3 and 4) sleep and disrupt the REM-NREM cycle. These sleep effects weaken with nightly use. When the drug is stopped after a few nights, REM sleep rebounds with vivid dreams or nightmares, and normal sleep may take several nights to return. Morning hangover is common.

cards.front: Why do thiopentone and phenobarbitone differ so much in duration of action?
cards.back: Duration depends on lipid solubility, redistribution, metabolism and excretion. Thiopentone enters the brain within seconds and redistributes to fat and muscle, so consciousness returns in minutes, although its eventual half-life is about 9 hours. Phenobarbitone enters the CNS slowly, is partly excreted unchanged in urine, and has a half-life of about 80 to 120 hours. Alkalinising the urine increases its excretion.

cards.front: How is acute barbiturate poisoning managed?
cards.back: Supportive care comes first: a patent airway, assisted ventilation, oxygen, fluids and vasopressors if needed, with dopamine preferred for renal perfusion. Gastric lavage with a charcoal suspension left in the stomach limits absorption. Alkaline diuresis helps mainly for long-acting, renally excreted barbiturates. Haemodialysis or haemoperfusion over activated charcoal removes both long- and short-acting drugs. There is no specific antidote.

cards.front: Short note: Barbiturate mechanism at GABA-A receptor

Prolongs the lifetime of GABA-opened Cl- channels (benzodiazepines increase opening frequency)
At high concentrations directly opens Cl- channels (GABA-mimetic)
Also reduces glutamate AMPA responses and Ca2+-dependent transmitter release

cards.front: Short note: Barbiturate poisoning: treatment and why dialysis works

points: Flabby coma, shallow respiration, falling BP, cardiovascular collapse, renal shutdown, bullous eruptions
Gastric lavage and activated charcoal; airway and ventilation; fluids and vasopressors (dopamine favoured for renal vasodilation)
Alkaline diuresis (sodium bicarbonate) helps only long-acting barbiturates eliminated renally
Haemodialysis or haemoperfusion over charcoal removes both long and short acting barbiturates; no specific antidote

cards.front: Short note: Barbiturate enzyme induction and interactions

points: Induces several CYP isoenzymes (CYP3A4/5, CYP2D6, CYP2C8/9, CYP2B6) and UGTs; also autoinduces
Reduces effect of warfarin, steroids including contraceptives, tolbutamide, griseofulvin, chloramphenicol, theophylline
With alcohol, antihistamines and opioids

cards.front: Short note: Barbiturates: CNS actions, tolerance and why they were replaced

points: Dose-dependent CNS depression: sedation, sleep, anaesthesia, coma
Hangover, impaired learning and memory; no selective anxiolytic action
Cellular and enzyme-induction tolerance; fatal dose not greatly increased
Withdrawal: excitement, hallucinations, delirium, convulsions; deaths reported
Narrow margin and abuse liability; benzodiazepines have a higher therapeutic index, lower ceiling depression and less enzyme induction

cards.front: Why are benzodiazepines safer than barbiturates?
cards.back: Benzodiazepines are selective modulators rather than global CNS depressants, so their depression has a lower ceiling. Even large overdoses usually leave consciousness and breathing largely intact, whereas barbiturate overdose causes coma and respiratory failure. They also distort sleep architecture less, cause less rebound and dependence, and do not induce hepatic enzymes the way barbiturates do.

cards.front: Classify the drugs acting at the benzodiazepine site: agonist, inverse agonist and antagonist.
cards.back: Agonists such as diazepam increase GABA-induced chloride influx and produce sedation and anxiolysis. Inverse agonists such as DMCM reduce GABA action and are convulsant. Flumazenil is a competitive antagonist that blocks both, so it reverses both sedative and convulsant effects at this site. Picrotoxin blocks the chloride channel directly rather than acting at the benzodiazepine site.

cards.front: Classify: drugs at the GABA-A complex
cards.text: Benzodiazepines increase the {{frequency}} of chloride channel opening, barbiturates increase its {{duration}}, and {{flumazenil}} is the competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine site.

cards.front: Benzodiazepine receptor and anticonvulsant facts
cards.text: Flumazenil is a {{competitive}} BZD antagonist; zaleplon and zolpidem bind the {{alpha-1}} subunit isoform; the BZD receptor increases the {{frequency}} of Cl- channel opening.

cards.front: Flumazenil: what is its profile and main uses?
cards.back: It is a benzodiazepine analogue with little intrinsic activity of its own. It acts within seconds after IV injection and lasts 1 to 2 hours, with an elimination half-life of about 1 hour, so resedation can occur. It is not given orally. Uses are reversal of benzodiazepine sedation after anaesthesia or procedures, and as an adjunct in benzodiazepine overdose alongside supportive care. It also reverses the hypnotic effect of zolpidem-type drugs.

points: Dizziness, ataxia, disorientation and anterograde amnesia
Slowed reaction time: unsafe to drive the next day
Hangover is less common than with barbiturates but occurs with long-acting drugs or larger doses
Complex sleep behaviours (sleepwalking, sleep driving) with no memory of the event
Paradoxical excitement, irritability and nightmares, especially with flurazepam and nitrazepam
Older patients are more prone to psychomotor effects
Tolerance to sedation develops, but dose escalation is uncommon
Low abuse liability; drug seeking is not prominent
Withdrawal is usually mild: anxiety, insomnia, restlessness; convulsions are rare
Worsen obstructive sleep apnoea: avoid
Additive CNS depression with alcohol and other depressants
Caution with sodium valproate, where psychotic symptoms have been reported

cards.front: Short note: Flumazenil

cards.front: Why do barbiturates have a steeper toxicity risk than benzodiazepines?
cards.back: Barbiturates are general CNS depressants that depress respiration, lower BP and cardiac output at higher doses, and cause respiratory failure and collapse. Benzodiazepines have a lower ceiling of CNS depression and a high therapeutic index; patients stay arousable and seldom need assisted breathing.

cards.front: Short note: Benzodiazepine receptor and GABA-A modulation (agonists, inverse agonists, flumazenil)

alpha-1 subunit: sedation, hypnosis, amnesia; alpha-2: anxiolysis and muscle relaxation

cards.front: Short note: Benzodiazepine adverse effects, dependence and withdrawal

points: Dizziness, vertigo, ataxia, amnesia, slowed reaction time: no driving
Sleep walking and sleep driving with no memory of events
Elderly more susceptible to psychomotor effects; can aggravate sleep apnoea
Abuse liability lower than barbiturates; withdrawal milder but possible (alprazolam withdrawal marked)
Flumazenil, a specific BZD antagonist

cards.front: Why do benzodiazepines lower BP differently on i.v. injection?
cards.back: Diazepam and lorazepam lower BP by reducing cardiac output; midazolam lowers it mainly by decreasing peripheral resistance. Diazepam also dilates the coronary arteries transiently.

cards.front: Why are zolpidem, zaleplon and eszopiclone called non-benzodiazepine hypnotics?
cards.back: They are chemically unrelated to benzodiazepines but act at benzodiazepine receptors that contain the alpha-1 subunit, which mediates hypnosis and amnesia. Because they lack meaningful anxiolytic, muscle relaxant and anticonvulsant action, their hypnotic effect is more selective. They have lower abuse potential, and their hypnotic action is reversed by flumazenil.

cards.front: What are the roles of melatonin and ramelteon in sleep disorders?
cards.back: Melatonin acts on MT1 and MT2 receptors to set the timing of the sleep-wake cycle. Low doses (2 to 10 mg) mainly shift the propensity to sleep, which helps jet lag, shift work and delayed sleep phase syndrome, but it is not a dependable hypnotic. Ramelteon is a selective MT1/MT2 agonist taken about 30 minutes before bed for sleep-onset insomnia. It has no GABA action and no benzodiazepine-type effects, and CYP inhibitors such as fluvoxamine raise its levels.

cards.front: Classify: benzodiazepine hypnotics by duration
cards.text: Long-acting hypnotic benzodiazepines include {{flurazepam}} and {{nitrazepam}}; short-acting ones include {{triazolam}} and {{temazepam}}, and {{alprazolam}} is a short-acting agent with a short-lived active metabolite.

cards.front: Classify: non-benzodiazepine and orexin-based hypnotics
cards.text: {{Zolpidem}} and {{zaleplon}} act on alpha-1 containing benzodiazepine receptors; {{zopiclone}} has a half-life of about {{5 to 6 hours}}; {{suvorexant}} is a dual {{orexin}} receptor antagonist.

cards.front: Classify: melatonin receptor agents
cards.text: Melatonin acts on {{MT1 and MT2}} receptors; {{ramelteon}} is a selective agonist at these receptors, taken about {{30 minutes}} before bed for {{sleep-onset}} insomnia.

cards.front: Short note: Sedation, hypnosis and general anaesthesia as grades of CNS depression

points: Sedative: calms and subdues excitement without sleep; decreased responsiveness and alertness
Hypnotic: induces and maintains sleep resembling normal arousable sleep
Hypnotics have quick onset, short duration and steep dose-response; sedatives are slower with flatter curves
High hypnotic doses produce general anaesthesia; a low hypnotic dose may act as a sedative
Treatment of insomnia is the most important use of this drug class

cards.front: How should a hypnotic be chosen for sleep-onset insomnia versus frequent night waking?
cards.back: For difficulty falling asleep, use a rapidly absorbed, short-acting agent taken late enough to avoid morning sedation. For frequent night waking, a longer-acting agent such as flurazepam or nitrazepam may be used, accepting some daytime sedation. Long-acting drugs and those with active metabolites accumulate on nightly use and cause next-morning impairment. Choose by pharmacokinetic profile, use the lowest effective dose and keep the course short.

cards.front: Short note: Stages of normal sleep and drug effects on them

points: Stage 1 (dozing) 3 to 6%; stage 2 (unequivocal sleep) 40 to 50%, spindles and K complexes
Stages 3 and 4 (slow wave sleep) 5 to 8% and 10 to 20%; difficult to arouse
REM (paradoxical) 20 to 30%; dreams, irregular eye movement, erection in males
Stages 0 to 4 and REM recur over 80 to 100 min
Benzodiazepines lengthen stage 2 and shorten stages 3 and 4; they distort architecture less than barbiturates
Barbiturates cut REM and stages 3 and 4; rebound REM and nightmares follow withdrawal

points: Differ more than 50-fold; redistribution explains short action of lipophilic drugs despite long elimination half-life

Short acting (triazolam, temazepam, alprazolam): shorter effect, fewer residual effects

cards.front: Why are hypnotics contraindicated in obstructive sleep apnoea?
cards.back: Patients with obstructive sleep apnoea already sleep poorly and feel sleepy by day; all hypnotics aggravate the apnoea, so they are contraindicated.

Sleep hygiene and regular sleep-wake times
Avoid daytime napping, caffeine and alcohol; relaxation and stimulus control
Treat the underlying somatic or psychiatric illness
Match onset and duration to the sleep problem
Next-day impairment depends on dose and kinetics
Short-term use limited to about 2 to 3 weeks
Hypnotics for chronic insomnia are of uncertain value
Intermittent use (for example every third night) may be tried

cards.front: Short note: Triazolam, midazolam and the problem of short-acting hypnotics

points: Very potent; peak under 1 hour; good for induction but poor for maintenance
Rebound insomnia and early morning anxiety; withdrawn in the UK but used elsewhere for elderly, shift workers and travellers
Peak about 20 minutes; ataxia and blackouts in the elderly; abuse liability
Not an oral hypnotic now; used as i.m. premedicant or i.v. anaesthetic

cards.front: What is the typical presentation and EEG pattern of absence seizures?
cards.back: Brief episodes, usually in children, lasting about half a minute. The child stares and freezes with no or only momentary loss of consciousness and no fall. The EEG shows a generalised 3 per second spike-and-wave pattern. Several episodes may occur daily, and seizures often remit in adolescence.

cards.front: Classify: drugs for absence seizures
cards.text: {{Ethosuximide}} blocks the {{T-type calcium}} current in thalamocortical neurones; {{valproate}} is a first-line drug for absence seizures; {{clonazepam}} is used as an adjuvant but tolerance develops within about {{six months}}.

cards.front: Short note: Classification of epileptic seizures and the drug of choice for each

points: Tonic-clonic (GTCS), absence (3 Hz spike and wave, children), atonic, myoclonic, infantile spasms
Simple partial: consciousness kept; complex partial (temporal lobe): confusion and amnesia
Partial may secondarily generalise into GTCS
Absence: ethosuximide or valproate (valproate first-line)
Myoclonic: valproate most effective; atonic: valproate
CPS: carbamazepine most effective; GTCS and partial: carbamazepine, valproate, phenytoin

cards.front: What are the key rules for starting and stopping antiseizure therapy?
cards.back: Start early with a single drug at low dose, raise gradually, and switch gradually, lowering the old drug as the new one is raised. Combine drugs only after monotherapy fails, preferably with different mechanisms. Withdraw gradually (except for toxicity), since abrupt stoppage can precipitate status epilepticus.

cards.front: Short note: Antiseizure drugs in pregnancy

points: Do not stop drugs in a pregnant woman: seizures themselves harm the foetus through anoxia
Withdrawal carries a high risk of status epilepticus

Phenytoin: foetal hydantoin syndrome (phalanx, cleft palate, microcephaly)

Folic acid in the second and third trimesters to reduce neural tube defects
Vitamin K in the last month to prevent neonatal bleeding
Seizures during pregnancy cause anoxia and can harm the foetus and cause later mental retardation
Fits during pregnancy increase the risk of birth defects in the offspring

Alumina cream on monkey motor cortex

cards.front: How are febrile convulsions managed, and why was chronic phenobarbitone prophylaxis dropped?
cards.back: Keep temperature down with paracetamol and cooling. Best treatment is rectal diazepam at the onset of convulsions (i.v. preparation if rectal not available); intermittent diazepam from the onset of fever is advised in recurrent or high-risk cases. Chronic phenobarbitone prophylaxis was abandoned because of poor efficacy and behavioural side effects.

cards.front: Essay: Classification and mechanisms of antiseizure drugs

Treatment depends mainly on seizure type, not aetiology
Generalised: tonic-clonic, absence, myoclonic, atonic, infantile spasms
Partial: simple, complex (temporal lobe) and secondarily generalised
Maximal electroshock: tests spread of discharge; active against tonic-clonic and complex partial seizures
PTZ clonic seizures: tests the focus; active against absence and myoclonic seizures

Sodium channel: phenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, lacosamide

Valproate and topiramate act at several targets, which explains their breadth
Lamotrigine combines sodium channel and presynaptic glutamate effects
Agents with different mechanisms are combined when monotherapy fails
Newer drugs are better tolerated but less well studied

cards.front: Essay: Principles of antiseizure drug therapy

points: Total seizure control at an acceptable level of side effects
About half of patients achieve full control; 20 to 30% partial control; the rest are refractory
Select by seizure type and individual need
Newer drugs are less sedating with fewer interactions, but less well studied
Start one drug at low dose and titrate to full control or side effects
If the maximum tolerated dose fails, substitute, reducing the first drug gradually
Add a second drug only if monotherapy fails; combine drugs with different mechanisms
Steady-state plasma levels guide dosing: individual variation and poor compliance are common
Keep the regimen simple and maintain a seizure diary
Treatment is usually long term, at least 3 years after the last seizure
Withdrawal should be gradual; favourable features include childhood onset and normal EEG
Recurrence after withdrawal is 12 to 40%
A single unprovoked seizure with no risk factors may not need treatment
Pregnancy: continue therapy; supplement folic acid and vitamin K
Febrile convulsions: rectal diazepam at onset; phenobarbitone prophylaxis abandoned
Prevent injury; place in prone or lateral position with airway patent
Most attacks end in 2 to 3 minutes; patient may not be fit to drive for hours

cards.front: How does phenytoin block seizures at the cellular level?
cards.back: It prolongs the inactivated state of voltage-gated sodium channels, which limits high-frequency repetitive firing while leaving normal low-frequency activity largely unchanged. At therapeutic levels it does not alter resting membrane potential or normal synaptic transmission. Its effects on glutamate release and calcium entry need higher concentrations, so their contribution is uncertain.

cards.front: List the chronic adverse effects of phenytoin.
cards.back: Gum hypertrophy is the commonest, more common in younger patients, and oral hygiene reduces it. Others are hirsutism, coarsening of facial features, acne, rashes or lupus-like reactions, and rarely neutropenia. Long-term use can cause megaloblastic anaemia through folate malabsorption and osteomalacia through impaired vitamin D activation. Exposure in pregnancy can cause foetal hydantoin syndrome.

cards.front: Classify: phenytoin pharmacokinetics
cards.text: Phenytoin is hydroxylated by {{CYP2C9 and 2C19}} with {{capacity-limited}} kinetics; its therapeutic range is about {{10 to 20 mcg/ml}}, and its half-life can rise to about {{60 hours}} at higher levels.

cards.front: Why does phenytoin plasma level rise disproportionately with small dose increments?
cards.back: Its hepatic hydroxylation (mainly CYP2C9 and 2C19) is capacity limited, so clearance shifts from first-order to zero-order over the therapeutic range. Once levels exceed about 10 mcg/ml, the half-life lengthens from 12 to 24 hours towards about 60 hours. Small dose increases then produce large rises in concentration, so plasma level monitoring guides dosing.

cards.front: Short note: Phenytoin - kinetics, toxicity and interactions

points: Oral absorption is slow because of poor aqueous solubility; bioavailability varies between products
Fosphenytoin is a water-soluble prodrug; dosed as phenytoin equivalents
Hydroxylation by CYP2C9 and 2C19 with capacity-limited, zero-order kinetics
Therapeutic range about 10 to 20 mcg/ml; toxicity above 20 mcg/ml (mild) and above 35 mcg/ml (severe)
Half-life lengthens sharply at high levels
Chronic: gum hypertrophy, hirsutism, acne, folate deficiency, osteomalacia
Dose-related: nystagmus, ataxia, diplopia, drowsiness, confusion, nausea
Rapid IV injection: hypotension and arrhythmias; phlebitis; extravasation causes necrosis
Inducer of CYP2C8/9 and 3A4; competitive inhibitor of CYP2C9/19
Raised levels with valproate (protein displacement), chloramphenicol, isoniazid, cimetidine, warfarin
Reduced levels of oral contraceptives, steroids, doxycycline, theophylline; sucralfate reduces absorption

cards.front: Short note: Phenytoin: mechanism, why it does not raise PTZ threshold and why it suits GTCS

points: Prolongs inactivated state of voltage-gated Na+ channel; suppresses high-frequency firing, not normal firing
Little sedation; no effect on resting potential or normal transmission
Abolishes tonic phase of MES; does not raise PTZ threshold; does not prevent kindling
Also used in trigeminal neuralgia and cardiac arrhythmias (high-frequency suppression)

cards.front: Short note: Phenytoin pharmacokinetics: non-linear kinetics and monitoring

points: Hydroxylation by CYP2C9 and CYP2C19 plus glucuronidation; capacity limited (first order changes to zero order)
Small dose rises give disproportionate plasma rises; half-life rises from 12 to 24 h up to 60 h above 10 microgram/mL
Plasma level monitoring guides dosing
Slow oral absorption due to poor aqueous solubility

cards.front: Short note: Phenytoin toxicity: gingival hyperplasia, foetal hydantoin syndrome and i.v. risks

points: Gum hypertrophy (commonest, about 20%, younger patients; reduced by oral hygiene)
Hirsutism, coarsened features, acne; rash, DLE, lymphadenopathy; rare neutropenia
Folate interference (megaloblastic anaemia) and vitamin D activation (osteomalacia)
Foetal hydantoin syndrome (hypoplastic phalanges, cleft palate, microcephaly), probably from an arene-oxide metabolite
Vein injury, thrombosis, extravasation necrosis; fall in BP and arrhythmia need ECG monitoring

cards.front: Short note: Phenytoin interactions

points: Potent inducer of CYP2C8/9 and CYP3A4/5; competitively inhibits CYP2C9/19
Valproate (protein binding displacement), chloramphenicol, isoniazid, cimetidine, warfarin
Sucralfate binds it in gut; carbamazepine induces its metabolism (phenobarbitone effect unpredictable)
Reduces oral contraceptive efficacy, doxycycline and theophylline levels; competitively inhibits warfarin

cards.front: What acute (dose-related) toxic effects does phenytoin cause, and what extra hazards come with i.v. injection?
cards.back: Overdose gives cerebellar and vestibular signs (ataxia, vertigo, diplopia, nystagmus), then drowsiness, confusion, hallucinations and rigidity, plus epigastric pain, nausea and vomiting. i.v. phenytoin sodium injures the vein (intimal damage, thrombosis, limb oedema, necrosis if it leaks) and can cause hypotension and arrhythmias, so ECG monitoring is needed.

cards.front: Essay: Phenytoin - pharmacology, kinetics, uses and toxicity

points: Synthesised in 1908 as a barbiturate analogue; found anticonvulsant in the electroshock model in 1938
Not a global CNS depressant; only mild sedation at therapeutic doses
Prolongs inactivation of voltage-gated sodium channels
Blocks high-frequency firing; spares normal activity
Also explains use in trigeminal neuralgia and cardiac arrhythmias
Slow oral absorption; hepatic hydroxylation by CYP2C9 and 2C19
Capacity-limited kinetics; half-life 12 to 24 hours, up to about 60 hours at high levels
Plasma monitoring is essential; small dose changes cause large level changes
Previously the standard drug for generalised tonic-clonic and partial seizures
Now reserved when better-tolerated drugs cannot be used
Can worsen absence and myoclonic seizures
Gum hypertrophy, hirsutism, acne, rash, megaloblastic anaemia, osteomalacia
Cerebellar and vestibular toxicity; confusion and hallucinations at high levels
Foetal hydantoin syndrome in pregnancy
Many interactions through enzyme induction and inhibition, and protein displacement
Fosphenytoin is a water-soluble prodrug given at a faster rate; can be given in saline or glucose

cards.front: Which drug is the first choice for trigeminal neuralgia, and why does it work?
cards.back: Carbamazepine. It selectively reduces high-frequency nerve firing that drives the temporal summation of pain impulses, so it has an almost diagnostic effect in these neuralgias, unlike a general analgesic. About 60% of patients respond well. Phenytoin, lamotrigine and baclofen are less effective alternatives, and gabapentin may be tried in non-responders. It is not useful for diabetic or other neuropathic pain.

cards.front: What are the mechanisms and spectrum of valproate?
cards.back: Valproate is broad spectrum. It prolongs sodium channel inactivation in a frequency-dependent way, weakly reduces the T-type calcium current, raises brain GABA by inhibiting its breakdown and possibly by increasing synthesis, and blocks NMDA-type glutamate receptors. It is the drug of choice for absence, myoclonic and atonic seizures, and a first-line drug for generalised tonic-clonic and partial seizures.

cards.front: What are the key features of lamotrigine?
cards.back: It is a broad-spectrum drug with a carbamazepine-like profile: it prolongs sodium channel inactivation and may reduce the release of glutamate and aspartate. It is used for partial and generalised tonic-clonic seizures, and also for absence and myoclonic seizures. Valproate doubles its level by inhibiting glucuronidation, so the dose should be halved when valproate is added; lamotrigine in turn lowers valproate levels. A severe rash, especially in children, requires withdrawal.

cards.front: Classify: sodium channel-acting antiseizure drugs
cards.text: {{Phenytoin}}, {{carbamazepine}}, {{oxcarbazepine}}, {{lamotrigine}} and {{lacosamide}} act mainly by prolonging sodium channel inactivation, whereas {{ethosuximide}} acts on T-type calcium current.

cards.front: Which seizure types can carbamazepine worsen, and why does that limit its use?
cards.back: It can exacerbate myoclonic, absence and atonic seizures. It is the most effective drug for complex partial seizures and widely used for tonic-clonic and simple partial ones, so the seizure type must be identified before choosing it.

cards.front: What happens to carbamazepine's half-life with chronic use, and which drugs does it affect?
cards.back: Its half-life falls from 20 to 40 hours at first to about 10 to 20 hours on chronic use, because it induces its own metabolism. It is oxidised to an active 10,11-epoxide and is an inducer of CYP3A4 and 2C9. It lowers levels of valproate, lamotrigine, oral contraceptives and haloperidol, and phenytoin and phenobarbitone induce it in turn. Erythromycin, fluoxetine and isoniazid raise its levels.

cards.front: What are the serious risks of valproate?
cards.back: Fulminant hepatitis is rare but serious and occurs mainly in children below 3 years, especially those with liver disease, on other antiseizure drugs or on other hepatotoxic drugs; liver function should be monitored. Given in pregnancy it has caused spina bifida and other neural tube defects, so it should be avoided. Concurrent carbamazepine raises the risk of foetal abnormalities. Concurrent clonazepam is contraindicated because absence status may be precipitated.

cards.front: Short note: Carbamazepine: uses, mechanism and toxicity

points: Na+ channel inactivation similar to phenytoin; raises threshold to PTZ and electroshock; inhibits kindling
Lithium-like effect in mania; antidiuretic effect (enhances ADH on renal tubule)
Most effective for CPS; widely used for GTCS and SPS; drug of choice for trigeminal neuralgia (about 60% respond)
Can worsen myoclonic, absence and atonic seizures
Dose-related: sedation, dizziness, diplopia, ataxia (extended-release tablets reduce peaks)
Hypersensitivity: rash, hepatitis, lupus-like, rarely agranulocytosis and aplastic anaemia
Hyponatraemia in elderly; valproate combination doubles teratogenic risk

cards.front: Short note: Carbamazepine as enzyme inducer and its interactions

points: Metabolised by CYP3A4 and CYP2C9; autoinduces, so half-life falls from 20 to 40 h to 10 to 20 h
Haloperidol, oral contraceptives, lamotrigine, valproate, topiramate
Erythromycin, fluoxetine, isoniazid

cards.front: Short note: Valproate: mechanisms, uses and hepatic and fetal risks

points: Frequency-dependent Na+ channel prolongation; weak T-current block; more GABA by inhibiting GABA-transaminase and synthesis; NMDA blockade
Drug of choice for absence; first line for GTCS and partial; most effective for myoclonic; atonic; mania alternative to lithium; migraine prophylaxis
Fulminant hepatitis rare, mainly under 3 years; alopecia, weight gain, bleeding; neural tube defects (avoid in pregnancy)

cards.front: Short note: Phenobarbitone as an antiepileptic: efficacy and drawbacks

points: Raises seizure threshold, limits spread, suppresses kindling; higher anticonvulsant to hypnotic ratio than other barbiturates
GTCS, SPS and CPS; status epilepticus IM or IV but slow to act; not for absence or atonic seizures
Sedation wanes but anticonvulsant action persists; learning and memory impairment; hyperactivity in children

cards.front: Short note: Ethosuximide: absence seizures and the T-current

points: Suppresses PTZ clonic seizures at doses without other effects; ineffective on MES and kindling
Selectively blocks the thalamic low-threshold T-type Ca2+ current that drives 3 Hz spike and wave
Absence seizures primary; approved for myoclonic seizures; valproate now preferred
GI intolerance, tiredness, mood change, headache, inability to concentrate

cards.front: Short note: Clonazepam and clobazam: benzodiazepine antiepileptics

points: Blocks PTZ seizures; ineffective in GTCS; used for absence, myoclonic and akinetic epilepsy and acute mania
Tolerance develops within about six months; sedation and salivation adverse effects
1,5-benzodiazepine; useful in partial, GTCS, absence and atonic seizures including refractory cases
Adjunct to carbamazepine, valproate or lamotrigine; active metabolite half-life over 35 h

cards.front: Short note: Primidone: a prodrug that works through phenobarbitone

points: Deoxybarbiturate converted to phenobarbitone and phenylethyl malonamide (PEMA); these active metabolites give the effect
Seldom used now; adjunct to phenytoin or carbamazepine in GTCS and partial seizures
Phenobarbitone-type effects; rarely anaemia, leukopenia, psychosis, lymph node enlargement

cards.front: Short note: Carbamazepine: mechanism, adverse effects and recent advances

points: Acts like phenytoin on sodium channels, prolonging the inactivated state
Inhibits high-frequency firing; presynaptic action reduces transmitter release
Inhibits kindling
Slow, variable oral absorption; about 75% protein bound
Oxidised to an active 10,11-epoxide; induces CYP3A4 and CYP2C9
Half-life falls with chronic use because of autoinduction
Dose-related sedation, dizziness, diplopia and ataxia
Rash, photosensitivity, hepatitis, lupus-like syndrome; rarely agranulocytosis and aplastic anaemia
Hyponatraemia in the elderly through enhanced ADH action; minor foetal malformations
Oxcarbazepine: active metabolite is not oxidised, so less epoxide toxicity and enzyme induction; more hyponatraemia
Newer antiseizure drugs such as perampanel, retigabine, stiripentol and rufinamide are second-line or add-on

cards.front: Short note: Valproate interactions: why clonazepam combination is contraindicated

points: Phenobarbitone and lamotrigine (metabolism inhibited); unbound phenytoin rises when valproate displaces it
Contraindicated: may precipitate absence status epilepticus
Foetal abnormalities more common when valproate and carbamazepine are used together

cards.front: Essay: Non-epileptic uses of antiepileptic drugs

points: Several antiseizure drugs also suppress high-frequency neuronal firing or modulate pain and mood pathways, so they have uses beyond epilepsy
Drug of choice for trigeminal and related neuralgias; it works by cutting temporal summation of high-frequency impulses, not as an analgesic
Not useful in diabetic, traumatic or other neuropathic pain
Alternative to lithium in mania and bipolar illness
Mania and bipolar illness (divalproex is mainly for this)
Migraine prophylaxis
First-line for diabetic neuropathy and postherpetic neuralgia
Gabapentin: migraine prophylaxis and trigeminal neuralgia in nonresponders; phobic states alternative
Topiramate: migraine prophylaxis
Phenytoin, lamotrigine and baclofen: less effective alternatives in trigeminal neuralgia

cards.front: A child has absence and generalised tonic-clonic seizures. Why choose valproate over carbamazepine?
cards.back: Valproate covers absence, myoclonic, atonic and tonic-clonic seizures and is the drug of choice for generalised types. Carbamazepine is very effective in partial and tonic-clonic seizures but can worsen myoclonic, absence and atonic seizures. Valproate carries hepatic and teratogenic risk (neural tube defects) and raises levels of phenobarbitone and lamotrigine, so weigh these, especially in girls of child-bearing age.

cards.front: What are the mechanism and main uses of gabapentin and pregabalin?
cards.back: They are GABA derivatives that do not act at GABA-A receptors. They modulate calcium channels containing the alpha-2-delta subunit, which may reduce glutamate release, and gabapentin may also enhance GABA release. They are add-on drugs for partial seizures. Gabapentin is first-line for neuralgic pain, such as diabetic neuropathy and postherpetic neuralgia. Gabapentin has no drug interactions and is excreted unchanged in urine, with a half-life of about 6 hours.

cards.front: Classify: newer antiseizure drugs by target
cards.text: Levetiracetam binds {{SV2A}}; gabapentin and pregabalin act on {{alpha-2-delta}} calcium channel subunits; tiagabine blocks {{GAT-1}}; vigabatrin inhibits {{GABA transaminase}}.

cards.front: How do tiagabine and vigabatrin each raise GABA activity?
cards.back: Tiagabine blocks the GAT-1 transporter that clears released GABA into neurones and glia, so GABA lingers in the synapse. Vigabatrin inhibits GABA-transaminase, the enzyme that degrades GABA, so GABA levels rise. Both are add-on drugs for partial seizures; vigabatrin is also used in infantile spasms.

cards.front: Why is topiramate called a broad-spectrum antiseizure drug, and what are its notable adverse effects?
cards.back: It acts by several mechanisms: prolongs Na+ channel inactivation, potentiates GABA postsynaptically, blocks certain glutamate receptors and hyperpolarises via K+ channels, so it works in partial, generalised tonic-clonic and some myoclonic or absence seizures. It is also a weak carbonic anhydrase inhibitor. Adverse effects: poor attention and memory, word-finding difficulty, sedation, ataxia, weight loss, paraesthesias, renal stones. It is also approved for migraine prophylaxis.

cards.front: Explain the mechanism and interaction profile of levetiracetam.
cards.back: It binds the synaptic vesicle protein SV2A, which may alter release of glutamate and GABA, and it inhibits N-type calcium channels. It is not oxidised by CYP enzymes and does not induce or inhibit them, so it has no pharmacokinetic interactions. It is mainly excreted unchanged in urine with a half-life of 6 to 8 hours. Side effects are sleepiness, dizziness, weakness and occasional behavioural change. It is not approved below 4 years.

cards.front: Short note: Newer antiseizure drugs grouped by mechanism

points: Lacosamide: enhances slow inactivation; CYP2C19; adults only, add-on for partial seizures
Oxcarbazepine and eslicarbazepine: act through an active monohydroxy metabolite; eslicarbazepine once daily
Zonisamide also suppresses repetitive firing
Tiagabine blocks GAT-1 reuptake; add-on for partial seizures
Vigabatrin inhibits GABA transaminase; reserve drug, used in infantile spasms
Clobazam is a 1,5-benzodiazepine with a long-lived active metabolite
Levetiracetam binds SV2A; no CYP interactions
Gabapentin and pregabalin act on alpha-2-delta calcium channel subunits
Topiramate: weak carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, Na+ channel effects, GABA potentiation, glutamate antagonism; prophylaxis of migraine
Zonisamide: weak carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, T-type calcium current block; avoid in sulfonamide allergy

cards.front: Short note: Oxcarbazepine and eslicarbazepine: why they are better tolerated than carbamazepine

points: Converted to a glucuronide-conjugated active metabolite; no epoxide, so fewer epoxide toxic effects
Weak enzyme inducer; fewer interactions; hyponatraemia more common; lower hepatotoxicity risk
Dose for dose less potent than carbamazepine
S(+) prodrug giving the same active metabolite; once-daily dosing; adjunct for partial seizures in adults
Initial 400 mg/day, up to 1200 mg daily

cards.front: Zonisamide: what do its mechanism and adverse effects tell you about who should avoid it?
cards.back: It prolongs Na+ channel inactivation and suppresses T-type Ca2+ current, and is a weak carbonic anhydrase inhibitor. That explains metabolic acidosis and renal stones. It is a sulfonamide, so avoid it in sulfonamide-sensitive patients. Long half-life (over 60 h), mostly excreted unchanged, no drug interactions noted.

cards.front: Lacosamide: mechanism, place in therapy and why it is convenient to combine
cards.back: It enhances Na+ channel inactivation and suppresses repetitive firing, so it works like phenytoin and carbamazepine at the channel. It is used only as add-on in adults for partial seizures. It neither induces nor inhibits drug-metabolising enzymes, so companion drug doses need no change. Adverse effects: ataxia, vertigo, diplopia, tremor, depression and cardiac arrhythmia.

cards.front: Essay: GABA modulators in epilepsy

points: GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter; enhancing it is one of the main ways antiseizure drugs work, alongside Na+ channel inactivation and Ca2+ current block
Benzodiazepines (clonazepam, clobazam, diazepam, lorazepam) raise the frequency of GABA-A channel opening
Phenobarbitone prolongs channel opening
Topiramate adds a postsynaptic GABA potentiating effect
Tiagabine blocks GAT-1 reuptake
Vigabatrin inhibits GABA-transaminase
Valproate inhibits GABA degradation and probably raises synthesis from glutamate
Gabapentin and pregabalin: GABA enhancement and alpha2-delta Ca2+ channel modulation; which one accounts for the effect is not known
Combining a Na+ channel drug with a GABA-facilitating drug is the rational combination
Benzodiazepines suit emergencies and adjunct use; tolerance and sedation limit chronic use

cards.front: What is the first-choice drug for status epilepticus, and what is the dose?
cards.back: IV lorazepam, 0.1 mg/kg (about 4 mg in adults), injected at no more than 2 mg/min. It can be repeated once after 10 minutes if needed. It controls seizures in 75 to 90% of cases with a sustained effect of 6 to 12 hours, because it is less lipid soluble and redistributes more slowly than diazepam. Thrombophlebitis is also less likely. The airway, glucose and oxygenation should be secured at the same time.

cards.front: Classify: status epilepticus drugs
cards.text: Lorazepam is given IV at {{0.1 mg/kg}} at no more than {{2 mg/min}}; fosphenytoin is infused at {{100 to 150 mg/min}} up to a maximum of {{1000 mg}} under ECG monitoring.

cards.front: How is status epilepticus defined, and why is it an emergency?
cards.back: Seizure activity lasting over 30 min, or two or more seizures without recovery of consciousness in between. Repeated tonic-clonic convulsions can cause death and permanent brain damage, so fits must be stopped as fast as possible after airway and general support.

cards.front: Short note: Status epilepticus management

points: Maintain airway, oxygenation and intubation if needed
Give IV dextrose to correct possible hypoglycaemia
Monitor BP, cardiac rhythm, fluid and electrolytes
Lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV at no more than 2 mg/min; repeat once after 10 minutes
Diazepam 0.2 to 0.3 mg/kg IV is the older standard, but its effect fades after about 20 minutes and it damages the vein more
Rectal diazepam is used where IV access is not possible
Fosphenytoin 100 to 150 mg/min IV up to 1000 mg, with ECG monitoring; given whatever the lorazepam response
Phenytoin only when fosphenytoin is unavailable, at 25 to 50 mg/min
Phenobarbitone 50 to 100 mg/min IV up to 10 mg/kg as an alternative
Failure of lorazepam and fosphenytoin within about 40 minutes of onset
Treat with IV midazolam, propofol or thiopentone anaesthesia, with or without curarisation, in intensive care

cards.front: Short note: Diazepam: the all-purpose benzodiazepine

points: Anxiolytic, hypnotic, muscle relaxant, premedicant, anaesthetic adjunct, emergency seizure control
Rapid oral absorption helps both sleep onset and maintenance
Only BZD with analgesia on i.v. use; reduces nocturnal gastric secretion; short coronary dilatation on i.v. injection
Diazepam and lorazepam are highly effective for short-term status epilepticus; tolerance limits long-term anticonvulsant use

cards.front: Why is fosphenytoin preferred over phenytoin for intravenous use?
cards.back: Fosphenytoin is a water-soluble prodrug converted to phenytoin in the body. It causes less intimal injury, can be infused faster (150 mg/min), and can be given in saline or glucose, unlike phenytoin, which precipitates in glucose. Doses are in phenytoin equivalents and ECG monitoring is still needed.

cards.front: Why is diazepam used for emergency seizures but not for long-term epilepsy?
cards.back: Diazepam is strongly anticonvulsant and acts fast, so it is first line for emergency convulsions (status epilepticus, tetanus, eclampsia, convulsant poisoning). Long-term use is limited by sedation and rapid tolerance to the antiepileptic effect; slow IV injection can cause thrombophlebitis.

cards.front: Why is lorazepam better suited than diazepam for status epilepticus?
cards.back: Diazepam is rapidly redistributed, so its effect is less sustained; it also causes more local thrombophlebitis. Lorazepam is less lipid soluble and redistributes slowly, giving more sustained action (about 6 to 12 h) and less thrombophlebitis, so it is the first-choice benzodiazepine in status epilepticus. Diazepam remains a first-line drug for emergency convulsions generally (tetanus, eclampsia, convulsant poisoning).

cards.front: Essay: Stepwise drug therapy of status epilepticus and why each drug is placed where it is

points: Airway, oxygenation and general support first; control fits quickly
Benzodiazepine i.v.: lorazepam preferred for lasting effect and less thrombophlebitis; diazepam rapidly redistributes
Fosphenytoin i.v. is given after the benzodiazepine regardless of response: it may stop fits lorazepam did not control and starts long-term therapy
Fosphenytoin replaces phenytoin: less vascular damage, faster infusion rate, can be given with saline or glucose; both still need ECG monitoring
Phenytoin sodium only if fosphenytoin is unavailable; it must go slowly, causes more local vascular injury and precipitates in glucose
Phenobarbitone i.v. is slower acting; an alternative to fosphenytoin or used if it fails, and to hold seizure-free state before oral therapy
Fits not controlled by lorazepam and fosphenytoin within about 40 min: i.v. midazolam, propofol or thiopentone anaesthesia in intensive care
Never stop antiseizure drugs abruptly; withdrawal can precipitate status

cards.front: Essay: Newer antiseizure drugs: mechanisms, approved uses and safety flags

points: Introduced as second-line or add-on drugs for refractory partial seizures in some countries (KDT8 ch30)
Each drug has its own warning profile, covered below (GG14 ch20)
Lacosamide enhances Na+ channel inactivation
Cenobamate: enhances Na+ inactivation and may block persistent Na+ current (GG14 ch20)
Tiagabine blocks GAT-1; vigabatrin inhibits GABA-transaminase (KDT8 ch30)
Levetiracetam and brivaracetam bind SV2A
Perampanel is a noncompetitive AMPA receptor antagonist (GG14 ch20)
Topiramate and zonisamide: weak carbonic anhydrase inhibitors
Gabapentin and pregabalin modulate a subset of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (KDT8 ch30)
Cannabidiol, rufinamide, stiripentol, ezogabine: target-specific actions, Dravet and Lennox-Gastaut niche (GG14 ch20)
Lacosamide: 17 years and older, add-on for focal-onset seizures (GG14 ch20)
Brivaracetam: adults and adolescents 16 years and older, add-on
Perampanel: focal seizures, 12 years and older
Rufinamide: Lennox-Gastaut, 4 years and older
Cannabidiol: Lennox-Gastaut, Dravet and tuberous sclerosis seizures (US, 1 year and older)
Perampanel: anxiety, confusion, aggression, suicidal thoughts
FDA suicidality warning applies to all antiseizure drugs
Cenobamate: shortens QT (avoid if short QT), DRESS risk
Felbamate: aplastic anaemia and hepatitis, so last-line
Ezogabine: retinal changes and skin/lip pigmentation
Choose by seizure type, age and interactions; monitor for the drug-specific warning

cards.front: What is perampanel and what is it used for?
cards.back: First-in-class noncompetitive AMPA-type glutamate receptor antagonist. Add-on for focal-onset seizures in patients 12 years and older. Long half-life (about 105 h) allows once-daily dosing.

cards.front: Short note: Perampanel

points: Noncompetitive AMPA antagonist; reduces fast excitatory signalling
Adjunct in focal-onset seizures, with or without secondary generalisation, 12 years and older
Starts at 2 mg once daily; maximal dose 4 to 12 mg/day at bedtime
Anxiety, confusion, imbalance, visual disturbance, aggression, suicidal thoughts
Metabolised by hepatic CYP3A

cards.front: Short note: Brivaracetam compared with levetiracetam

points: Both bind SV2A, a synaptic vesicle protein
Brivaracetam has higher affinity for SV2A and also inhibits voltage-gated Na+ channels
Approved as adjunct for focal-onset seizures in patients 16 years and older (2016)
Dose 50 mg BD, adjustable to 25 mg BD by response and tolerability (GG14 ch20)
Metabolised by CYP2C19 and 2C9; does not induce or inhibit CYP enzymes (GG14 ch20 table)

cards.front: Short note: Cenobamate

points: Enhances fast and slow Na+ channel inactivation; may inhibit persistent Na+ current (GG14 ch20)
Partial-onset seizures in adults, as monotherapy or add-on; dose-dependent response in refractory cases
Half-life 30-76 h; may be non-linear at higher doses
Metabolised by CYP2E1, 2A6 and 2B6
Shortens QT interval: contraindicated if QT is already short
Allergic reactions and DRESS (eosinophilia and systemic symptoms)
Somnolence, dizziness, diplopia, headache are common

cards.front: What is cannabidiol used for in epilepsy?
cards.back: A non-intoxicating plant-derived (phytocannabinoid) antiseizure drug approved in the US for seizures of Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, Dravet syndrome and tuberous sclerosis complex (age 1 year and older). Metabolised by liver and intestinal CYPs.

cards.front: What is rufinamide and what is its main use?
cards.back: A triazole derivative, structurally unrelated to other antiseizure drugs. Adjunct for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome seizures, 4 years and older. It is added to other drugs because it is approved only as adjunctive therapy.

cards.front: What is stiripentol and why does it need dose checks of companion drugs?
cards.back: An aromatic alcohol, structurally unrelated to other antiseizure drugs, used in Dravet syndrome with clobazam and valproate. It is a GABA-A allosteric modulator and inhibits CYP1A2, 3A4, 2C19 and 2D6, so companion drug levels can change.

cards.front: Why is felbamate restricted to last-line use?
cards.back: Its serious risks are aplastic anaemia and hepatitis (it carries a boxed warning). It is approved only for focal seizures not controlled by other drugs.

cards.front: What is ezogabine (retigabine) and what warning applies to it?
cards.back: A potassium channel opener that enhances KCNQ (Kv7) currents. Warnings: retinal abnormalities and skin and lip pigmentation, which may be permanent.

cards.front: Essay: Melatonin: physiology, receptors and therapeutic potential

points: Principal hormone of the pineal gland, secreted at night
Made from serotonin by N-acetylation and O-methylation (GG14 ch15)
Entrains the sleep-wake cycle to the circadian rhythm
Acts on MT1 and MT2 receptors, both GPCRs, to start sleep and fix its timing (KDT8 ch29)
Ramelteon: MT1/MT2 agonist for sleep-onset insomnia; no GABAergic action, no BZD-like side effects; 8 mg before bed; low bioavailability from first-pass metabolism
Tasimelteon: for non-24-hour circadian disorder in totally blind patients (GG14 ch22)
Benefit of supplements is unproven, though sold as a health food; secretion declines with age
Ramelteon levels rise with fluvoxamine, ciprofloxacin, fluconazole; rifampicin lowers them
Melatonin receptor agonists fit circadian and sleep-onset problems, not general sedation

cards.front: What is tasimelteon used for?
cards.back: A selective MT1/MT2 melatonin receptor agonist (it fixes circadian timing), used for non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder in totally blind patients. The FDA approval also covers non-blind users, though no trials were done in them.

cards.front: How is melatonin made in the pineal gland?
cards.back: From serotonin, by N-acetylation followed by O-methylation. It is secreted mainly at night and entrains the sleep-wake cycle to the circadian rhythm.

cards.front: What is cenobamate?
cards.back: A newer antiseizure drug for partial-onset seizures in adults, as monotherapy or add-on. It acts mainly through sodium channel effects and reduces focal seizures in a dose-dependent way.

cards.front: Which amino acids are the inhibitory neurotransmitters of the CNS?
cards.back: GABA is the main one. Glycine is the other fast inhibitory amino acid; taurine and beta-alanine also act as inhibitory amino acids. GABA and glycine both open chloride channels.

cards.front: Where does glycine act as an inhibitory transmitter?
cards.back: Mainly in the spinal cord and medulla, where it opens chloride channels. One site is the Renshaw cell to motoneurone junction, which inhibits antagonist muscles.

cards.front: Which general anaesthetics and sedatives enhance glycine-mediated inhibition?
cards.back: Barbiturates, propofol and many inhalational anaesthetics. They augment glycine-mediated inhibition; ketamine and N2O do not act on glycine or GABA-A channels.

cards.front: How does GABA-B activation differ from GABA-A activation?
cards.back: GABA-A is a fast chloride channel. GABA-B is a metabotropic G-protein receptor: it opens K+ channels and closes presynaptic Ca2+ channels, so it slows the neurone and cuts transmitter release. Baclofen is a GABA-B agonist.

cards.front: Short note: Inhibitory amino acid neurotransmitters and drugs acting on them

points: GABA: main inhibitory transmitter of the CNS
Glycine: inhibitory mainly in the spinal cord and medulla
Taurine and beta-alanine: also inhibitory amino acids
GABA-A and glycine receptors: pentameric chloride channels, hyperpolarising and fast
GABA-B: metabotropic G-protein receptor; closes presynaptic Ca2+ channels and opens K+ channels
Benzodiazepines increase the frequency of channel opening
Barbiturates prolong opening and can activate the channel directly
Propofol and inhalational anaesthetics potentiate GABA-A
Barbiturates, propofol and inhalational anaesthetics augment glycine inhibition
Strychnine blocks glycine inhibition, causing reflex tonic-clonic convulsions
Baclofen: GABA-B agonist used as a skeletal muscle relaxant
Sodium oxybate (GHB): acts on GABA-B and extrasynaptic GABA-A receptors; used for narcolepsy cataplexy (GG14 PDF p548)
Flumazenil blocks the benzodiazepine site on GABA-A

cards.front: Short note: Withdrawing an antiseizure drug

points: GG14: continue at least 2 years, then consider tapering if seizure-free
KDT8: therapy may be life-long or at least 3 years after the last seizure
Childhood epilepsy
No family history of epilepsy
Primary generalised tonic-clonic epilepsy
Withdraw gradually, not abruptly, except when the drug is toxic
